questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: identify what a headline selects for attention out of a full report
questions.stem: An online news site rewrites the same city council report under three different headlines, each of which stresses a different part of the story. Which statement about the three headlines is accurate?

options.text: Each headline selects one fact from the report and puts it first, so the three differ in what the reader is asked to think about first
The three headlines report three separate council decisions, because a site may not reuse one report under several titles
options.misconception: assumes a rule against reusing one report, when a single document under several titles is standard practice and is how more readers meet it

options.text: The three headlines differ only in length, so the longest one carries the most detail for a reader in a hurry
options.misconception: reads character count as detail, when a short headline can carry a large claim and a long one can carry almost nothing

options.text: Only the first headline is the site's own work, and the other two are copied word for word from an agency feed
options.misconception: invents a provenance the page never offered, since a headline carries nothing that says who wrote it

questions.explanation: A headline is not a summary of a report, it is a selection from one, and the selection is the editorial act. All three headlines here are drawing on a single report and each puts a different fact in first position, which is why they produce three different first impressions from identical evidence. That is the whole basis on which a reader should compare them: ask which fact each one chose, and notice that a fact made to be a headline has to survive being separated from its context, so the most dramatic sentence in a report is often the one that was chosen. The distractors each assume a rule that does not exist. There is no restriction on reusing a report under several headlines, and doing so is a standard way of increasing the chance that a reader meets it. Length is not a measure of detail, since a short headline can carry a large claim and a long one can carry almost nothing. The last one is the story a reader might tell themselves, and it is unfalsifiable in the wrong direction: nothing in a headline says who wrote it, so a reader who assigns one title to a newsroom and the other two to an agency has invented a provenance the page never offered.
questions.hint: Ask which single fact each title leads with, and whether the three can all be true of one document.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: infer the audience an advertisement is aimed at from its evidence
questions.stem: A television commercial shows a product being used at night by two adults with no children in the frame, and the only spoken line is that it helps you sleep. Which inference about the advertisement is well supported?

options.text: The advertisement is built for adult buyers who are being sold a benefit, and the setting supplies the problem the product solves
The advertisement is aimed at everyone in the household, since no group has been excluded from the picture
options.misconception: treats the absence of a group from the frame as evidence that the advertisement is addressed to the whole household

options.text: The advertisement is aimed at children, since the product is presented without anyone speaking in a serious tone
options.misconception: reads a light tone as a signal about the audience, when tone says nothing about who is being addressed

options.text: The advertisement is aimed at sports buyers, since the product is shown in use during a period of the day people normally exercise
options.misconception: reads a time of day as a time of activity, when the night setting was chosen to fit a problem about sleep

questions.explanation: An advertisement has to be economical, so it never states its audience; it assumes the audience and then arranges the evidence for them. Here every choice points the same way: two adults and no children fixes the intended buyer as an adult rather than a parent shopping for a child, the night-time setting supplies the situation in which the promised benefit would be wanted, and a single spoken line avoids anything that would be wasted on a viewer who is not being addressed. A learner should be able to say what each element does, because that is the method: the picture is the problem, the product is the solution, and the line is the promise. The distractors each mistake absence of evidence for evidence. Not showing a group does not address everyone, and an advertiser who wanted the whole household would put a whole household in the frame. There is nothing childish about a light tone, and the absence of a serious voice says nothing at all. The last one reads a time of day as a time of activity, when the choice of night was made to fit a problem about sleep, not to place anybody in a gym.
questions.hint: Ask who is in the frame, what problem the setting shows, and what the single spoken line promises.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: explain why a post on a short-form platform is shaped as it is
questions.stem: A post of about twenty characters performs a small act and drops a piece of everyday vocabulary that a careful writer would avoid. Which reading of that choice is correct?

options.text: The limit on length rewards a message that is complete in a few words and rewards a familiar tone, and the platform does not reward a careful hedge
The limit on length is only a technical constraint, so the tone of the words is a separate matter that the platform has nothing to do with
options.misconception: severs the link between the length limit and the register, when a constraint on space is exactly what rewards a plain familiar tone

options.text: A short post cannot be a correct claim, so the informality should always be read as evidence that the content is unreliable
options.misconception: treats style as truth, when a confident tone is a property of a sentence and support is a property of a source

options.text: The limit on length forces writers to leave out the context that would let a reader check the claim, and that is the most likely reason a short claim feels stronger than it is
options.misconception: states a consequence as if it were the design, when crowding out the context is a side effect rather than the purpose of the limit

questions.explanation: A length limit is a design decision and it changes what counts as a good sentence. On a short-form platform a message has to finish inside a small space, which means the writer's skill moves from writing at length to choosing the one sentence that carries the whole act, and the reward goes to a tone a reader recognises as a person talking rather than an institution announcing. The dropped hedge is part of the same effect: a platform that scrolls past a qualifier rarely rewards one. The other three readings each break the link between the constraint and the effect. The length limit is not merely technical, because nothing technical explains the register, and the fact that the constraint shapes the language is exactly the point. C mistakes style for truth, which is a mistake worth naming as a habit, because a confident tone is a property of a sentence and a well-supported claim is a property of a source, and the two travel independently. D is the most interesting option and it is close, but it states the harm as if it were the design, when the effect of context being crowded out is a consequence rather than the purpose, and a learner who says so will be able to tell the two apart.
questions.hint: Ask which part of the sentence the length limit rewards, and whether informality is evidence about the claim or about the writer.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: recognise the disclosure a paid post is expected to carry
questions.stem: A creator posts a photo of a product with a long caption describing how much she uses it, and the post carries no word that says she was paid or given anything. Which judgement is fairest?

options.text: The post needs a disclosure, because a paid or gifted endorsement that reads as personal experience is the case a disclosure rule exists for
The post is fine as written, because the disclosure rule only applies to advertisements made by a company rather than by a person
options.misconception: narrows the rule to corporate advertisers, when a sponsored post by an individual is exactly the case readers mistake for experience

options.text: The post is fine as written, because nobody is harmed by one photo and a long caption is a small amount of text
options.misconception: measures the exposure by the length of the post, when the rule counts readers and not characters

options.text: The post does not need a disclosure, because a reader who notices the product in a photo has already been told the important fact
options.misconception: confuses noticing that a product exists with being told the creator was paid to praise it

questions.explanation: Disclosure rules exist for one reason: an endorsement is a piece of persuasion, and the person it persuades should be able to see whose interest produced it. The post in the stem is a long, warm, first-person account of using a product, which is the form that is hardest for a reader to read as an advertisement and the form a disclosure rule is aimed at. A person posting as herself is inside the rule as much as a company, because the difference between them is who pays, not whether the reader is being persuaded. The three distractors are all reductions, and each reduces the harm differently. B narrows the rule to advertisements, which is the error that the rule was written against, since a sponsored post by an individual is precisely the case where readers most easily mistake promotion for experience. C counts the size of the post, which the rule does not do; the exposure is measured in readers, not in characters. D is the subtlest, because the fact that a product is visible in a photograph is true and irrelevant, since what the reader needs is not to know that a product exists but to know that the person praising it was paid to be praising it.
questions.hint: Ask whether a reader could tell from the post alone whether the creator was paid or given the product.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: weigh an online review that has signs of manipulation
questions.stem: A restaurant listing has forty reviews, all five stars, all posted within one day, all without any mention of food. Which claim about the reviews is the most defensible?

options.text: The pattern of the reviews is itself evidence worth raising, whatever each individual review says
The reviews are still reliable, because a restaurant that receives five-star reviews deserves to receive them
options.misconception: argues from the restaurant's merit, which says nothing about whether the reviews were written independently

options.text: The reviews are unreliable, because a real customer would always mention the food somewhere
options.misconception: states a rule that is simply false, since plenty of real reviews rate a visit without describing a single dish

options.text: The reviews are unreliable, because five stars out of five is too high a score for a restaurant to be worth
options.misconception: treats a single high score as implausible, when implausibility lies in forty identical scores rather than in one

questions.explanation: A reader evaluating a review should look at the pattern before the prose, because the pattern is the part that manipulation cannot disguise. Forty reviews that are all at the maximum score, all arriving inside a single day, and all silent about the thing the listing is for, is a combination that organic reviews very rarely produce and coordinated ones produce constantly. That is a reason to treat the set as evidence worth raising, and the right verb is the quiet one. The distractors each overclaim in a different direction, and a learner should be able to name which kind of overclaim they have heard in the wild. B is the appeal to the restaurant's merit, which says nothing about the reviews, since a good restaurant can attract organised praise and a bad one can too. C states a rule that is simply false, because plenty of real reviews rate a visit without describing a single dish. D is the opposite error and the more common one in print: it treats a high score as inherently implausible, when five stars is a perfectly ordinary score and implausibility is a property of forty identical ones, not of one.
questions.hint: Ask what a normal set of reviews for a place like this would look like, and which detail of this set is out of step with it.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: read a vague attribution and name what it fails to establish
questions.stem: A report on a factory closure attributes the main fact to sources familiar with the matter rather than naming any of them. Which statement about that sentence is correct?

options.text: It marks the information as coming from a person rather than a document, and it withholds the name, so a reader cannot check the source
It reports the factory closure as settled fact, because an attributed statement has already been verified by the newsroom
options.misconception: assumes that publication is verification, when deciding a claim is safe to print is a different judgement from establishing it

options.text: It means the newsroom has several sources who agree, since a reporter will not write a single vague attribution
options.misconception: inverts the convention, since a vague attribution conceals a source rather than reporting agreement between several

options.text: It shows the closure is sensitive, because a reporter protects a named source out of courtesy
options.misconception: reads a protective convention as a positive signal about the claim, when protecting a name is a reason for the vagueness and not evidence for it

questions.explanation: Attribution is the part of a report that tells a reader where a claim came from, and a vague attribution such as this one is a deliberate reduction. It has two effects at once, and both matter. It marks the claim as coming from a person rather than from a document or a public record, which signals that the claim is not independently checkable from anything the reader can see, and it withholds the name, which removes the reader's ability to judge the source's position, access or motives. A reader who is being asked to accept a claim on trust should at least know they are being asked to. The distractors each read a protective convention as a positive guarantee, and it is worth being precise about why. B is the error of assuming that publication is verification; a newsroom that prints an attribution has decided it is safe to print, which is a different judgement from the claim being established. C inverts the convention entirely, since vagueness usually conceals a single source. D is the charitable reading, and it is not false, but it is also not what the sentence says: protecting a name is a reason for vagueness, and the vagueness is the effect, not the evidence of caution.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader can now verify, and what the writer chose not to let the reader see.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: state exactly what a fact-check establishes and what it leaves open
questions.stem: A fact-check site labels a claim false on the ground that a document it found does not say what the claim says. Which description of what has been verified is accurate?

options.text: The check establishes that the document does not support the claim, and it does not by itself establish that the claim's conclusion is false
The check establishes that the claim is false, and therefore that the opposite of the claim must be true
options.misconception: commits a false dilemma, since the failure of a document to support a claim says nothing about the opposite statement

options.text: The check establishes that the person who made the claim was lying, because a claim outruns its document
options.misconception: turns a sourcing problem into a state of mind, and no document can establish what a person believed

options.text: The check establishes that the document is genuine, because a forged document is the only way a claim can outrun one
options.misconception: diagnoses forgery that the evidence does not reach, since a claim can outrun a genuine document perfectly well

questions.explanation: The discipline in this field is the difference between a claim and its support, and a fact-check that keeps the two apart is doing its job properly. What has been established here is a fact about the relationship between a document and a sentence: the document does not say what the sentence says it says. That is a real finding and it is enough to stop a reader relying on the sentence as sourced. What has not been established is the negation of the sentence. A claim can be unsupported and still be true, and it is quite possible that the document found is the wrong document, or that the claim was checked against a source and a better one exists. The distractors each collapse a bounded finding into a much larger one. B is the false dilemma, because the failure of a document to support a claim says nothing at all about the opposite statement, which may also be unsupported. C turns a sourcing problem into a state of mind, and no document can prove what a person believed. D is a different error again, a diagnosis of forgery that the evidence does not reach.
questions.hint: Ask what was compared with what, and then ask what would have to be found to establish the opposite.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: identify the signal a ranking system sorts on
questions.stem: A short-video feed shows a learner the same kind of clip over and over, and every clip is one she watched to the end. Which explanation of that feed is the soundest?

options.text: The feed is probably ranking on the signal it can measure most easily, and completion is the one it gets for free
The feed has decided that this learner is a beginner, and beginners are shown simple content until they improve
options.misconception: invents a stored assessment of the learner that the pattern gives no sign of

options.text: The feed shows what it shows because the learner asked for this content in an earlier session
options.misconception: appeals to a stated preference, which would not produce a narrow set unless the platform had decided to act on it

options.text: The feed shows what it shows because the clips the learner watched were all uploaded on the same day
options.misconception: offers a coincidence in place of a mechanism, which is what a reader reaches for when the real explanation is harder to see

questions.explanation: A ranking system is a sort, and the first question about any sort is what it sorts on. Here the pattern gives the answer away, because completion is a signal a platform can read for free with no rating, no form and no interruption, which is precisely the sort of signal that systems prefer: cheap, immediate and plentiful. Once that is the signal, the repetition follows without anyone deciding to repeat anything, because what a learner finishes is what the system calls relevant. A learner should learn to ask this question of every feed they use: not what is being shown, but what behaviour is being maximised. The distractors each offer a story that makes the system look thoughtful. B invents an assessment of the learner that nothing in the pattern supports, and a system that kept a file on each person's level would not need the behaviour at all. C is the appeal to a stated preference, and a stated preference would not produce a narrow set unless the platform had decided to act on it. D is a coincidence dressed as a cause, and it is the kind of explanation a reader reaches for when a real mechanism is harder to see.
questions.hint: Ask what the system measures, and then what it calls a good result.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: distinguish the goal a feed is built to produce from the goal a reader has
questions.stem: A reader opens a video feed intending to look at a talk about gardens, and finds himself an hour later watching cooking clips he never searched for. Which statement best describes the situation?

options.text: The feed and the reader are optimising different things, and the signals the system can measure beat the purpose the reader brought
The feed has malfunctioned, because a working feed would have kept showing the talk the reader opened it for
options.misconception: asks a feed to be one-shot, which no interactive recommendation system can be without ceasing to recommend at all

options.text: The feed has done exactly what it was asked to do, because the reader stayed an hour and stayed an hour is a signal
options.misconception: proves the point circularly by treating the outcome as the input the reader gave

options.text: The reader has been given good recommendations, because the clips are related to gardening in a way he appreciates
options.misconception: assumes the reader and the system share an objective, which is the assumption the whole situation is about

questions.explanation: This is the single most useful idea to bring away from thinking about recommendation systems, and the stem contains the evidence for it. The reader brought a purpose and the feed delivered something else, and the two are not in conflict because they were never the same objective. A feed is tuned to maximise a measurable behaviour, and measurable behaviours are the ones a machine can count: how long a person stayed, whether they came back, what they tapped past. Those are not goals a reader sets, they are by-products a reader produces, and a system that maximises by-products will drift from purpose steadily and without ever deciding to. The distractors each preserve a comforting idea at the expense of the mechanism. B asks a feed to be one-shot, which no interactive system can be without ceasing to recommend at all. C and D both assume the reader and the system share an objective, and C proves it circularly by treating the outcome as the input. A learner who cannot spot the difference between what a system optimises and what they want will keep blaming themselves for the drift.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader arrived wanting, what the system could count, and whether those are the same thing.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: describe the mechanism that narrows what a person sees
questions.stem: A reader who has watched a few videos on one side of an argument now finds that nearly everything recommended to him agrees with him, and he has not searched for anything. Which mechanism accounts for this?

options.text: The system is optimising for signals of agreement, and each agreeing clip is another signal to do it again
The system has detected the reader's views and chosen to show only material that confirms them, out of a wish to please him
options.misconception: gives the system a motive, and nothing in the feedback loop actually requires one

options.text: The videos that agree are the only ones about the topic, so the diversity is missing from the material rather than from the selection
options.misconception: makes a claim about the world that the reader could go and check by looking for what is being left out

options.text: Other readers have posted complaints, and the platform has removed the disagreeing videos from circulation
options.misconception: invents a censorship step, and it is the most damaging explanation because it hands a mechanical effect to a decision somebody took

questions.explanation: The bubble is produced by a feedback loop, and the loop is worth being able to state in one sentence: a signal was measured, the signal was rewarded, and the reward taught the system what to measure next. Watching to the end is such a signal, agreement is such a signal, and every clip that matches both produces more of them, so the narrowing is a consequence of optimising rather than an intention. That is the important part, because a bubble that nobody built still behaves as though somebody did. The distractors each supply an intention or an external force, and the point of the item is that neither is needed to explain the pattern. B gives the system a motive, and it is the motive people most often assume, but nothing in the loop requires it. C is a claim about the world that would have to be true, and it is the one a reader can actually check: look for the disagreeing material that is being left out. D invents a censorship step, which is the explanation that is most damaging when believed, because it transfers a mechanical effect to a decision somebody took.
questions.hint: Ask what behaviour the system rewarded last time, and what it will therefore reward next time.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: state what a hashtag does beyond the words it follows
questions.stem: A post ends with a short invented phrase preceded by a number sign, and the same phrase appears on thousands of other posts. Which statement about that mark is the most useful description of its job?

options.text: It groups posts that are not otherwise connected, so that people who do not follow one another can still find each other
It makes the post look official, because a mark before the words is a sign that a moderator has read the post
options.misconception: guesses at a status signal, and the truth is the reverse since whoever invents the phrase in a post is starting the group

options.text: It increases the length of the post, which is what platforms count when they decide how much to show a reader
options.misconception: treats the mark as padding, which a reader can test by comparing a post with one and a post without one

options.text: It hides the words from anyone who searches for them, because the mark is read as a rule against indexing the phrase
options.misconception: guesses at a technical rule that works the other way round, since the mark is what lets the platform pull the whole set out at once

questions.explanation: The useful way to think about a hashtag is that it is an index that the poster writes into the post rather than something a platform adds afterwards, and it does a job that no amount of tagging by the reader can do. A post that nobody follows is invisible to everyone except the people already present, and a shared phrase removes that dependence: the platform now has a key under which this post can be filed, and any reader who searches that key will find it, including people who have never heard of the poster. This is why the same invented phrase on thousands of posts behaves like a venue. The distractors are all guesses about a mark whose actual job is mundane and practical. B is a guess about status, and the truth is the opposite, since the person who invents a phrase in a post is the person starting the group. C treats the mark as padding, and a reader can test that by looking at whether a post with a hashtag and a post without one behave differently. D is the interesting one, because it is a common worry and the answer is technical: the mark separates the phrase from ordinary words so that the platform can recognise it as a key and pull the whole set out at once.
questions.hint: Ask what the mark gives the post that the words alone would not, and who can now find it.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: describe how a livestream differs from a recorded post in what a viewer can do
questions.stem: A livestream and an ordinary video post cover the same subject. Which difference in what a viewer can do follows from the fact that one is live?

options.text: A viewer can address the person making the content and receive an answer while the content is still happening
A viewer can return to any point in the content at will, because a live stream is stored in full before it is shown
options.misconception: attributes to a live stream the replay that only recorded and searchable video offers, which is what makes a stream an event

options.text: A viewer can guarantee that what is said is accurate, because nothing can be said live that would be edited out
options.misconception: is false in both directions, since nothing is cut from a live stream and nothing makes what is said true either

options.text: A viewer can see other viewers, so that a stream is a much stronger check on what is being said than a single comment
options.misconception: mistakes a display feature for a fact about accuracy, and a room full of people believing the same false thing is still wrong

questions.explanation: Live means the two ends of the exchange are in the same moment, and everything else about a livestream follows from that one fact. A viewer can put a question into the stream and have it noticed and answered while the topic is still open, which is why a livestream is a format for persuasion and teaching rather than for reference. That is the only real structural difference here, and it is worth knowing because it changes what a viewer is doing: participating rather than consulting. The three distractors each attribute a property that belongs to a different format or to none of them. B is a property of recorded and searchable video, and a stream is the least replayable thing a platform offers, which is exactly what makes it a live event. C is simply false in both directions, since nothing is edited out of a live stream and nothing makes what is said true either. D is a property some platforms do have, and a learner who has seen comments scroll past may assume it is universal, but the presence of other viewers is a display feature, not a fact about accuracy, and a room full of people believing the same false thing is still wrong.
questions.hint: Ask what the word live forces to be true about the timing of a viewer's message and the maker's reply.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: identify what a speaker must supply that a reader does silently
questions.stem: A speaker freezes on a recording while writing the same material goes smoothly, and a skilled talker freezes while writing out a talk that went well. Which explanation accounts for both?

options.text: A reader supplies structure silently and a listener cannot, so work a writer does without noticing becomes work a speaker has to say out loud
Speaking and writing use different vocabularies, so a person who has mastered one has not mastered the vocabulary of the other
options.misconception: explains the difficulty as a gap in vocabulary rather than as a gap in structure, and a speaker with the words and no signposts still loses listeners

options.text: A recording is judged harder than a page, so speakers freeze under a standard that written work never has to meet
options.misconception: claims a difference in standard where there is none, since the medium is harder rather than the test stricter

options.text: Writing puts the material in order before the speaker meets it, so a talker who writes loses the chance to find the order while speaking
options.misconception: has a kernel of truth but the wrong mechanism, since writing supplies an order rather than removing the chance to find one

questions.explanation: The medium takes something away from the listener, and what it takes is the scaffolding a reader builds without noticing. A reader sees a heading and knows where they are, can drop a clause and return to it, and can find the verb again after a long parenthesis; none of that survives in speech, because the ear cannot go back and cannot skim. Every one of those silent acts is therefore an explicit job for a speaker, who has to signpost in words, repeat a subject that has changed, summarise before moving on, and restate a point that was interrupted. The distractors each offer a reason that sounds familiar. B is a real difference between the media and it does explain some discomfort, but it explains it as a gap in vocabulary rather than as a gap in structure, and a speaker who has the words and no signposting still loses listeners. C claims a difference in standard where there is none, since the standards are the same and the medium is simply harder. D is the only one with something in it, but the mechanism is wrong: writing does not remove the chance to find an order while speaking, it supplies one in advance.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader does silently that a listener cannot do at all, and write the four jobs down.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: identify the constraint that shapes the design of a video call
questions.stem: A video call is usable for conversation and painful for anything that needs precise coordination between two people, and the difference is not the picture quality. Which explanation accounts for that?

options.text: The time between what one person says and the other sees or hears it cannot be made to zero, and coordination fails when the two sides are not acting at the same instant
The compression used on the picture reduces detail, so precise coordination fails because the faces are not clear enough to read
options.misconception: offers a real limitation that is not the one in question, since a blurred face can still be followed in a conversation

options.text: The microphones in ordinary rooms pick up too much echo, so coordination fails because neither side can hear the other properly
options.misconception: offers a room-dependent problem that would not produce a clean divide between talking and coordinating

options.text: The bandwidth required for two-way video is limited, so coordination fails because the connection cannot carry both directions at once
options.misconception: invents a one-way limit where connections do carry both directions, and varies too much by room to explain the effect

questions.explanation: The constraint that matters is delay, and the reason it matters is that conversation assumes that two people act on the same instant. Say a word and the other person replies, and the reply is timed against a moment that has already passed by however long the round trip took. Small delays are absorbed, because a reply that is slightly late still fits the turn, and this is why a call across a building works perfectly well. Coordination has no such slack. If two people need to be in the same place at the same moment, a delay between what one does and what the other perceives is not absorbed, it is a gap, and the gap has to be closed by looking rather than by doing. So a call is good for talk and bad for anything where a hand has to be in the same place as an object. The distractors are all real limitations and none of them is the one that produces the effect described. Lower picture detail does not stop two people coordinating, and a blurred face can still be followed in a conversation. Echo and bandwidth both vary by room and connection and neither one would produce a clean divide between talking and coordinating.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to a reply timed against a moment that has already gone, and which activities have no slack for that.

questions.learningObjective: identify which skill a situation actually calls for out of several neighbouring skills
questions.stem: A student receives a message saying that her school account will close tonight unless she verifies her details through a link, and she has never seen the sender's address before. Which skill is the situation testing?

options.text: Judging whether a message is trustworthy, which is a different skill from producing well-formed digital text
Writing digital text, because the reply she sends has to be correctly spelled and clearly punctuated
options.misconception: names a production skill while the wrong move in the situation is to compose anything at all

options.text: Organising files, because she needs to find the message later among everything else in her inbox
options.misconception: names a retrieval skill for a message she has already found

options.text: Managing a device, because the account is stored on a phone she has to configure before the deadline
options.misconception: names a setup skill for an account that is not hers to configure, and the deadline is not a configuration date

questions.explanation: Digital literacy is a bundle of separate skills, and the useful thing about the bundle is that the situations map onto the skills. This one is about judgement: the account, the deadline, the unfamiliar sender and the link form a set of signals, and the skill is knowing which of them to weigh. It is a decision made before any text is written and it is made about somebody else's text rather than her own. The distractors are all real components of the bundle and none of them is what the situation turns on, which is the reason this item is worth setting. Writing well-formed text is a production skill and nothing in the stem asks her to compose anything, since the wrong move is to reply at all. Organising files is a retrieval skill and the message has already been found. Managing a device is a setup skill and the account is not hers to configure. A learner who cannot separate the components tends to prepare for all of them, which is a way of solving nothing; the discipline is to ask which skill the situation is actually testing before deciding what to do.
questions.hint: Ask what the student has to decide before she writes or does anything, and what that decision is about.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: explain why length beats a short complex password
questions.stem: A person's account is protected by a long string of several ordinary words, and a colleague's by a short string of capital letters, digits and punctuation. Explain in your own words why the first is the harder one to break, and state the one practical rule that follows from the arithmetic behind it.

answer.exemplar: The reason is arithmetic, and it is worth stating the arithmetic because the rule is often believed for the wrong reason. The number of guesses a search has to make is the size of the alphabet raised to the power of the length. Adding capitals, digits and punctuation widens the alphabet, and widening a base does very little when the power is small: going from twenty-six possibilities to something near ninety is a multiplier of about three, which buys an attacker a few extra minutes. Adding four ordinary words to a passphrase multiplies the length instead, and length is the power, so the number of guesses rises by orders of magnitude rather than by a factor of three. The practical rule that follows is therefore to lengthen before complicating, and to treat a substitution of a capital letter for a lower-case one as a change that costs an attacker almost nothing. A second rule follows from the same place, which is that a long passphrase made of several words resists guessing far better than a short complex string, because the words can be long and the complexity can stay low. The point about guessing tools is worth adding because it explains the ceiling: a tool does not have to respect the advice, and it will try common substitutions early, so a password that depends on the difference between a letter and its capital is not a password that has been made stronger, it is one that has been made shorter in the only sense that matters.

questions.explanation: The exemplar is marked as correct for giving the exponent argument rather than an appeal to habit, for naming the substitution a guessing tool tries first, and for deriving a rule the reader can apply. A response that says long passwords are better because they are harder to guess has the right conclusion and the wrong reason, and the wrong reason is what the reader will forget.
questions.hint: Ask whether adding characters widens the alphabet or raises a power, and decide which of the two matters more when the password is short.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: The second factor in two-step verification
questions.learningObjective: name what the second factor is in a two-step verification scheme
questions.stem: An account asks for a password and then, separately, for a six-digit code sent to a phone the user already holds. What is the second factor, and what is it for?

options.text: Something the user has, and it is there to make a stolen password useless on its own
Something the user knows, and it is there to make the password longer without making the user type more
options.misconception: describes a change to the first factor, which leaves the failure it was meant to prevent completely untouched

options.text: Something the user is, and it is there to identify the person in the room as well as the account
options.misconception: describes a genuine second factor, but nothing in the scenario involves a body rather than a device

options.text: Something the user has done, and it is there to record that the account was used from a new device before it was allowed to work
options.misconception: describes a log entry, which records an attempt and stops nobody

questions.explanation: The two factors are a password you know and a code from a device you have, and the whole design rests on the fact that they fail in different circumstances. A password can be guessed, phished, reused from another site or handed over; a code sent to the phone cannot be reached without the phone. So an attacker who has stolen the password is stopped at the second step, which is exactly the situation the scheme exists for, and the six digits are deliberately short-lived so that a code observed once stops working within minutes. The distractors each name a real category of second factor, which is what makes the item worth setting, and each puts it in the wrong slot. B describes a longer password, which is a change to the first factor and leaves its failure modes untouched. C describes a fingerprint or a face, which is a genuine and common second factor, but nothing in the stem describes one. D is a record of the attempt rather than a check on the user, and a log entry does not stop anybody. A learner who can name the three categories and say which one this is will not confuse the terms again.
questions.hint: Ask what the second factor is a thing of, and what failure it is designed to stop.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: Signals that give away a phishing message
questions.learningObjective: select the reliable signals in a suspicious message
questions.stem: A message claims to be from a bank, warns that the account will be closed today, gives a link, and is written in a slightly odd register. Four of the five observations below are things a careful reader should actually weigh. Which four?

options.text: The pressure to act today, which removes the time in which a reader would normally check
The link, which a reader can inspect before going anywhere and does not need to open
The greeting that does not name the account, which is unusual for a real institution writing to one customer
The register, which is slightly wrong for the sender and is therefore a signal even though it is not proof
The length of the message, which is the measure most often used to decide whether a message is a forgery
options.misconception: borrows a connoisseur's technique, since judging a document by its length works on paintings and not on messages

questions.explanation: The four signals in the keyed set share a property worth naming, which is that each is checkable by the reader before any harm is done. The deadline removes deliberation, and deliberation is exactly what a fraudulent message needs to be short of. The link is directly inspectable without being followed, which is what makes it the most useful of the four. The unnamed greeting is a comparison against what a real institution usually writes to a customer, and the comparison is free. The register is weaker and the item is right to say so, since a slightly wrong register is a signal and not a proof, and a message written by a careful fraudster will have none. The fifth observation is the one to reject, and it is instructive that it is a real technique from elsewhere being borrowed: judging a forgery by its length belongs to connoisseurship, where the length of a document is evidence about a painting. It is not evidence about a message, because short genuine messages and long fraudulent ones are equally common, and a reader who weighs length will eventually meet a long forgery and start trusting it.
questions.hint: Ask which of the five the reader can check without acting on the message at all.

questions.learningObjective: order the stages of a fact-check into a working sequence
questions.stem: Four stages of a fact-check have been listed out of order by a class. Only one sequence is a workable order of work. Which sequence is it?

options.text: 把说法拆成可以一条一条核对的小部分 / 找出说法最初的来源 / 拿可靠的材料逐条对照 / 写出结论，说明哪些部分核到了、哪些没有

拿可靠的材料逐条对照 / 把说法拆成可以一条一条核对的小部分 / 找出说法最初的来源 / 写出结论，说明哪些部分核到了、哪些没有

questions.explanation: The workable order is the one in the first option, and each stage is placed where a reader would otherwise waste effort. Breaking a claim into parts comes first because it decides what the check is even about: a claim that has been taken apart can be checked part by part, and a claim that has not can only be checked as a lump, which is how a fact-check ends up verifying something nobody said. Tracing the origin comes second, because a claim is usually a distortion of something that exists and the distortion can only be measured against the original. Comparison with reliable material comes third, and it comes third on purpose: a checker who compares first is comparing against a guess. Writing the conclusion comes last, and the last clause of it is the part professional checkers insist on, namely the statement of what was not established, because a claim can be partly supported and the part that was not is where the misinformation usually is. The second option has the origin before the break-up, which costs time on a claim nobody yet knows the shape of. The third and fourth both write the conclusion before the comparison, which is the only sequence on the list that is not a method at all.
questions.hint: Ask what has to be decided before a comparison can be made, and what the last sentence of the conclusion is obliged to say.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: diagnose why a manipulated video is harder to check than a written claim
questions.stem: Stage one: a short clip shows a well-known person saying something they have never said, and the clip is indistinguishable from an ordinary one to the eye. Diagnose why a viewer cannot check this the way they check a written claim. Stage two: say what a viewer who suspects a clip should do instead of deciding on sight, and what makes that step better than conviction.

answer.exemplar: Stage one. A written claim leaves a trail that a reader can inspect, and a recording does not. In a sentence the parts are related to one another in ways that can fail: if a claim says a meeting happened on a Tuesday, a date on a document contradicts it, and the contradiction is visible to anyone who looks. In a recording there is no internal relation of that kind. A face is a face, a voice is a voice, and there is nothing inside the clip that says whether it was made or not, so the only evidence available is the surface, and the surface is exactly what has been manufactured. This is the reason the item is not simply a question about being alert, and the distinction matters for how much effort is worth spending. Stage two. The step that helps is a change of kind rather than a change of degree: stop examining the clip and go and look for the original statement somewhere else, in a channel the clip's author does not control. A published statement, a dated report, an earlier recording of the same event. This is better than conviction for a reason that is easy to state and easy to forget. Conviction is a feeling produced by watching, and a manufactured clip is designed to produce it. A search for the original is a test, and a test can come out against the suspicion, which a conviction never can. The two conclusions worth drawing are that the absence of visible signs is not evidence of authenticity, and that the right response to not being able to tell is to look elsewhere rather than to look harder at the same artefact.

questions.explanation: The pairing tests a diagnosis and a remedy. Marking the exemplar correct for locating the problem in the absence of an internal relation inside a recording, and for preferring an external comparison over a longer look, which is the move the field treats as sound.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader can inspect inside a sentence that there is no equivalent of inside a recording, and what happens if the search for the original finds nothing.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: The specific risk of public wifi
questions.learningObjective: name the risk that belongs to a network the user cannot authenticate
questions.stem: A traveller connects a laptop to the free network in an airport lounge and is warned about public wifi. Which risk belongs to that network specifically, as opposed to the general risk of using a computer in public?

options.text: Traffic on a network whose owner cannot be identified can be read or altered, because the connection is not authenticated at the other end
A stranger in the lounge can read the screen over the traveller's shoulder, which is a risk the network setting cannot address
options.misconception: blames the setting for a risk that is about the physical position of the machine and not about the connection

options.text: The network will use up the traveller's data allowance faster than a phone would, which is a cost rather than a risk to anything
options.misconception: confuses a billing consequence with a risk to the account or to what is being sent

options.text: The battery will drain faster while connected, which is a cost of using the network and not a reason to distrust it
options.misconception: names a power effect and then denies that it is a reason, so the option rules itself out

questions.explanation: The word that decides the risk is authenticated. A home or office network is one whose owner the connecting device can identify, usually by a password the owner set, and that is what tells the device it is talking to the right network. A free network in a lounge offers nothing of the kind: the device has no way to know who is on the other end, so the link is open and anything sent along it can be read or changed. The keyed answer describes that mechanism and nothing more, which is the discipline worth teaching. The other three options either name an effect the setting cannot touch or name one and then disqualify it. B is a real risk and it is a real risk, but it belongs to the room rather than to the network, and it is the reason a privacy screen is useful rather than a reason to distrust the connection. C and D are costs, and a cost is not the same thing as a way of losing something. A learner who has only heard that public wifi is dangerous often cannot say what is being endangered, and a warning without a mechanism is hard to act on.
questions.hint: Ask what the device cannot find out about the network it has just joined, and what follows from that.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: What a privacy setting actually changes
questions.learningObjective: distinguish what a privacy control changes from what a service still collects
questions.stem: A user turns off the setting that controls who can see her posts and later finds that her reading history is still visible to the service. Which reading of the setting is accurate?

options.text: The setting governs what other people are shown, and what the service itself records is a separate question the setting does not touch
The setting was set wrongly, because one control is supposed to cover both the audience of a post and the service's own record of it
options.misconception: treats the control as a single global switch, which is what stops a user looking for the other controls that exist

options.text: The reading history is kept for the convenience of the user, so it is not the service's data and the setting could not have covered it
options.misconception: moves the record across to the user by calling it convenient, which is the move that leaves it unexamined

options.text: The setting only takes effect after the account is closed, because services apply privacy changes at the end of a session
options.misconception: asserts a timing rule that does not exist, and it is the belief a distrustful user will adopt on principle

questions.explanation: A privacy control has a scope, and almost every misunderstanding of one comes from expecting it to be wider than it is. This control is about the audience: which other people are shown a post. What the service has recorded about the user is a separate question, stored separately, and no audience control touches it. That is why the user was not deceived and the setting did not fail. The distractors each restore the missing scope by assumption. B treats a control as if it were a single global switch, which is the belief that produces the worst outcome, because a user who believes one control is total will not look for the others. C is the charitable explanation and it is wrong in an instructive way: the record exists whether or not anybody enjoys it, and calling it the user's data rather than the service's data is exactly the move that leaves it unexamined. D is simply a false claim about timing, and it is the sort of thing a user who does not trust a service will believe on principle, so it is worth correcting explicitly rather than leaving.
questions.hint: Ask who the setting decides something is hidden from, and then ask separately who is keeping the record.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: What a free service is given
questions.learningObjective: identify what a free service takes in place of money
questions.stem: A user has not paid for a service and the company says the service is free. Which statement describes what the user has given in exchange?

options.text: Attention, and often the contents of what the user does there, which the company can sell to somebody else
Nothing, because a service that charges no money has no revenue and therefore no interest in the user
options.misconception: assumes no money means no interest, which is the assumption the whole arrangement is built to exploit

options.text: The right to read the user's messages, and only that, because a company with no revenue can only ask for one thing at a time
options.misconception: gives a partial answer with a false limit on it, and the limit is what makes the answer useless

options.text: Nothing at the moment, because a company is not permitted to sell anything until the user has actively agreed to it
options.misconception: states a consent rule that does not exist in that form, so the user assumes nothing is shared until agreeing

questions.explanation: A service that charges nothing is not a service with no customers; it is a service whose customers are the product. What it takes in place of money is the user's attention, and the mechanism by which attention becomes money is to work out who else would pay for access to this particular audience and to sell that access. The other half of the keyed answer is the one worth labouring: what the user does inside the service is itself the material, so the reading history, the searches and the connections are not incidental to the bargain but the thing being sold. The distractors each assume that no money means no interest, which is the assumption the whole business model is built to disprove. B is the error that lets a user agree to anything. C is a partial version of the truth with a false limit on it, and the limit is what makes it useless, because the value of a record grows with everything else in it. D states a rule that does not exist in that form, and a user who believes it will assume that nothing is shared until they actively agree, which is precisely backwards.
questions.hint: Ask who would pay to reach this user, and what material would be worth selling to them.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: assess how permanent a piece of posted material is
questions.stem: A user posts an angry message about a colleague, deletes it four minutes later, and moves on. Which assessment of what has happened is the most defensible?

options.text: The deletion removes the post, but a copy may already exist elsewhere, and anything kept in an archive does not come back when the original goes
The deletion removes the post completely, so nothing about it survives and the four minutes can be treated as never having happened
options.misconception: assumes the author's control extends to every copy, which stops at the moment the message was sent

options.text: The deletion removes the post but is visible to the colleague as a notification, so the useful effect is only to mark the message as withdrawn
options.misconception: gives a real effect as if it were the whole effect, and it reassures in exactly the way that will mislead next time

options.text: The deletion is delayed rather than refused, so waiting a few hours would have removed the message from every copy that now exists
options.misconception: invents a delay, and the promise that patience would have worked is what will lead to the same post being made again

questions.explanation: The reason deletion is unreliable is distribution, and a learner who has understood distribution will never again assume that a deleted post is gone. The moment something is posted, it has been sent to servers, to devices, to networks in between, and to services that archive on their own schedule without being asked, and none of those are under the author's control afterwards. The keyed answer is the one that says this and stops, which is the right level of confidence: it does not claim the message is certainly still visible, it says a copy may exist, and it distinguishes that from an archive, which is a third party's record and is not deleted by the author at all. The distractors each replace that with a clean story. B is the belief people act on and it is simply false, because a reader who saw the message has it. C is a real effect and it is not the whole effect, and it is oddly reassuring in a way that will mislead. D invents a delay, so it promises that patience would have worked, which is the belief that will lead somebody to post the same thing and delete it more slowly next time.
questions.hint: Ask how many copies of a sent message exist at the moment it is sent, and which of them the author can reach.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: identify the behaviour that makes a false claim travel
questions.stem: A claim that has been shown to be false keeps appearing in the feeds of people who have never met anyone who has corrected it. Which account of that spread is the soundest?

options.text: People pass on claims that fit what they already think, and the passing is a reward they get rather than a belief they have checked
People pass on claims that fit what they already think, because they have checked each one and decided it is the better answer
options.misconception: assumes a checking step that the act of sharing does not contain, and it is what makes sharing feel responsible

options.text: The claim is carried by a small number of accounts that post it constantly, and the reach comes from the volume rather than from agreement
options.misconception: explains the origin of one item rather than the persistence, and coordinated accounts do not carry a claim for months

options.text: The claim travels because the people who spread it are paid to, and removing the payment would remove the claim from the feeds
options.misconception: offers a remedy that is wrong, since the same payment structure carries accurate claims as well

questions.explanation: The mechanism that carries misinformation is the reward for sharing, and it is worth being exact about what the reward is, because getting this wrong produces the wrong remedy. It is not truth and it is not even belief. A person who shares a claim gets attention, agreement, or the sense of having contributed, and the cost of checking is real and immediate while the benefit of sharing is instant. The keyed answer says the passing is a reward rather than a conclusion, and that single change accounts for the pattern in the stem: the claim reaches people who have no connection to anybody who has examined it, because nothing in the act of sharing involves examining anything. The distractors each substitute a better story. B assumes a checking step that the behaviour does not contain, and it is the belief that makes people confident that sharing is responsible. C is often true of a given item and it does not generalise, because coordinated accounts explain the origin of a claim rather than why it is still being passed months later. D offers a remedy and the remedy is wrong, since the same payment structure carries accurate claims too.
questions.hint: Ask what the person who shares gains, and compare that with what checking would cost them at that moment.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: state what a screen-time report counts and what it therefore cannot tell a user
questions.stem: A user reads a report showing that an app accounted for four hours yesterday. Which statement about that figure is correct?

options.text: It counts time in the foreground, so an app left open behind another one is barely counted and nothing is said about what the user did while it was showing
It counts everything the app did, including work in the background, so four hours is a complete account of the app's use
options.misconception: assumes completeness, and background work is precisely the part of the use the figure leaves out

options.text: It measures attention rather than duration, so four hours of display corresponds to much less time in which the user was actually engaged
options.misconception: inverts the error by calling the report an attention measure, and the report supplies no factor to convert it into one

options.text: It counts the number of times the app was opened, and the figure has to be multiplied by an average session to obtain the time
options.misconception: names a different unit, and a reader can check for himself that the report gives no count of openings at all

questions.explanation: A measurement is defined by what it counts, and the most common misreading of a screen-time figure is assuming it counts the thing people care about. It counts foreground time, roughly from the moment an app becomes visible to the moment it stops being visible, which means two things follow. An app running quietly in the background is barely registered, so a total can understate the work an app really did. And the figure says nothing whatever about attention, because a screen showing a video for four hours and a screen showing a long article for four hours are the same number in the report and completely different experiences. The keyed answer states the counting rule and the consequence. The distractors each pick a different measure. B is the assumption of completeness that makes the number feel like an accounting, and background work is precisely what the number leaves out. C inverts the error, since the report is not an attention measure at all and there is no conversion factor in the report to make it one. D is a different unit entirely, and it is the one a reader can check for himself: the report does not give a count of openings, so nothing in it can be multiplied up to hours.
questions.hint: Ask what starts the clock and what stops it, and what the figure is silent about.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: identify an online norm and the behaviour it governs
questions.stem: A user is asked to follow a rule about answering other people's posts. Which pair of rule and behaviour it governs is coherent?

options.text: Answer in the same place the question was asked, because a public question left unanswered in public reads as a public refusal
Answer in a private message, because a disagreement that stays in public damages the person who asked in public
options.misconception: inverts the norm and produces exactly the public silence it was invented to prevent

options.text: Answer within a fixed number of minutes, because speed of reply is what a reader judges the answer by
options.misconception: makes timing the criterion, when a slow answer in the right place is still an answer and place is the norm

options.text: Answer everyone who writes, because leaving one person unanswered asserts a rank over the others
options.misconception: sets a rule about completeness that cannot be followed, and an unfollowable rule is not a norm

questions.explanation: An online norm is a rule about where a reply belongs, and the reason it exists is that the location of a reply is itself a public act. A question asked in a group is a request made in front of that group, and an answer sent privately answers a smaller audience than the one that asked. A reader who can see the question and cannot see the reply reads silence, and the silence is interpreted as a refusal that the asker chose to make in public. The keyed answer names the norm and the reason, and the reason is what makes the rule teachable rather than arbitrary. The distractors each sound plausible and none of them is a norm. B inverts it and produces exactly the failure the norm exists to prevent. C is about timing, which is a different concern and a much weaker one, because a slow answer in the right place is still an answer. D is a rule about completeness rather than about place, and it is also unworkable, since a user with a large account cannot answer everybody and a norm that cannot be followed is not a norm.
questions.hint: Ask who can see the reply, and compare that with who could see the question.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a repeated attack from a single disagreement
questions.stem: Two accounts of the same exchange are compared. In one, a person posts a reply disagreeing once and then does not return. In the other, the same person posts a reply every day for three weeks, each time naming the other person. Which distinction is the one that matters?

options.text: What separates them is repetition directed at a person rather than a reply, and a single disagreement can be sharp without being bullying
What separates them is the tone, so a rude single reply is bullying and a repeated polite one is not
options.misconception: makes tone the criterion, which labels a single rude remark as bullying and passes a repeated courteous attack

options.text: What separates them is the platform, so the same words are bullying on one site and an argument on another
options.misconception: claims the words change with the site, which lets the same conduct be excused by moving it somewhere else

options.text: What separates them is the audience, so bullying requires the post to be seen by many people and a private exchange cannot be either
options.misconception: depends the definition on a crowd, which lets a sustained attack pass because it happened quietly

questions.explanation: The distinction people most often get wrong is the one between a hostile remark and a sustained attack, and the two tests that matter are repetition and direction. Repetition is what makes it sustained: a single reply, however sharp, is a disagreement, and a person has a right to disagree badly once. Direction is what makes it an attack on a person rather than on a claim: the second account names the same individual day after day, and the content of the posts matters less than the fact that the target is the person. The keyed answer states both tests and adds the point learners most need, which is that a sharp single disagreement is not bullying. The distractors each pick one visible feature as if it were the definition. B makes tone the criterion, which will label a rude remark as bullying and let a repeated courteous attack through. C claims the words change with the platform, which is false and dangerously convenient, since it means the same conduct can be excused by changing where it happens. D is the one that lets the worst cases off, because the definition it proposes depends on a crowd, and it is a crowd that stops a sustained attack from working.
questions.hint: Ask how many times the exchange went one way, and what it was aimed at rather than at what it was about.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: connect a citizenship rule to the behaviour it actually governs
questions.stem: A school states the rule that a photograph of other people may not be posted without their permission. Explain what behaviour this rule governs, what it does not govern, and why a school would phrase it as a rule about permission rather than as a rule about what is fair.

answer.exemplar: The rule governs a single identifiable act: putting a photograph of another person in a place other people can reach. It is about publication rather than about possession, so keeping a picture of a colleague on a private phone falls outside it, and posting one to a group of two is inside it whether or not two feels like an audience. Everything else it appears to touch is outside it, and being able to say where the edges are is what makes a rule usable. It does not govern how a photograph is taken, it does not govern the content, since a flattering photograph and an unflattering one raise the same question, and it does not govern what a reader may then do with a photograph they have legitimately obtained. The last exclusion is the one that catches people, because consent to a post is not consent to a download. Why permission rather than fairness is the better formulation is the part of the answer worth most, and the argument is short. Fairness is a standard, and a standard has to be interpreted in every case, so two reasonable people apply it differently and the disagreement has nowhere to end. Permission is a fact about a particular act between two particular people, and a fact can be checked. A school that wants students to be able to reason about this for themselves therefore needs to hand them the concept of a permission rather than a series of judgements about what would have been decent, and the concept transfers to cases the school never thought of, including a picture taken by somebody else and reposted, which is the case most likely to reach a real student this year.

questions.explanation: The exemplar is marked as correct for drawing the boundary at publication rather than at possession, for naming the exclusion about what a reader may do next, and for arguing that permission transfers where a standard has to be re-argued each time. A response that only says the rule is about consent restates it and misses the argument the question asks for.
questions.hint: Ask whether the rule is about a picture or about a picture other people can reach, and ask what a standard would need that a fact does not.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: screen explanations of code-switching for ones that hold up
questions.stem: A bilingual speaker uses an English word inside a Chinese sentence when no English word exists for the thing being named. Four of the five explanations below are ones a linguist would accept. Which four?

options.text: The word names something recent, and the language that named it first is the shortest way to refer to it
The speaker is showing off, and bilingual speakers switch languages whenever they want to display their status
options.misconception: makes showing off the general motive, which is not the case and which teaches a listener to hear every switch as a boast

options.text: The concept is being discussed precisely because it is a new one, and the words in the other language are the ones already in the speakers' mouths
The switch marks a change of addressee, so the next person addressed is expected to know the other language
The switch happens only when the speaker is tired, so a careful speaker will never use a foreign word at all
options.misconception: confuses carefulness with avoidance, at the price of coining an awkward translation for a word everybody else borrows

questions.explanation: Three of these describe things that are actually going on, and the three are the ones worth teaching, because together they show that a switch is information rather than noise. The new-word explanation covers the commonest case: a thing arrived in one language, and the other language borrows the name along with the thing, so the speaker is being economical rather than lazy. The discussion explanation covers the related case in which the speakers are talking about the concept itself, and the words already in use are the ones in the other language. The addressee explanation is the one learners are least likely to believe, and it is easily testable in any bilingual household: a speaker changes language to match the person in front of them, which is a form of politeness, not a lapse. The two rejected explanations are the ones that moralise. Showing off as a motive is not the general case and a learner who believes it will hear every switch as a boast. The last is the belief that carefulness means avoiding a foreign word, and it is expensive: it is exactly the carefulness that makes a speaker coin an awkward translation for a word everybody else borrows, and the result is two communities calling the same thing different names.
questions.hint: Ask what the switch is doing for the listener, and separate the three explanations that survive from the two that moralise.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: A regional variety and a vocabulary difference
questions.learningObjective: read a vocabulary difference as a variety rather than as an error
questions.stem: Two speakers in different regions use different words for the same object and each is confident that their word is the real one. Which statement describes what the difference is?

options.text: It is a difference between the varieties of the language, and both speakers are using their own variety correctly
It is a difference in age, and the older speaker is using the older form while the younger one is being careless
options.misconception: reaches for age, which shows up as one speaker trying out a new term rather than as two confident adults

options.text: It is a difference in education, and the word used by the less educated speaker is the borrowed one
options.misconception: reaches for education, which mixes registers a person knows rather than producing a word only one region uses

options.text: It is a difference in formality, and the regional word is the casual form of the standard one
options.misconception: turns a variety into a casual register, and it teaches learners to avoid a word half the country says daily

questions.explanation: A vocabulary difference between regions is a difference between two systems that both work, and the test that distinguishes it from an error is simple: ask whether a speaker of the other region would understand the word, and if they would, nobody is wrong. The keyed answer says that, and it matters that it says both speakers are correct, because the alternative is to force one region to treat its own everyday speech as a mistake. The distractors each pick a variable that does real work in language and attach it to a case where it does not explain the observation. Age does drive lexical change, but an age difference shows up as one speaker trying out a new term, not as two adults each being confident. Education also shows up in vocabulary, and it does so by mixing registers a person knows rather than by producing a word only their region uses. The last is the one that does the most damage, because treating a regional word as a casual form of a standard one teaches learners to avoid a word that half the country speaks in daily life.
questions.hint: Ask whether a speaker of the other region would understand the word, and then ask which of the three variables would produce the difference.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: describe how a borrowed word changes on the way in
questions.stem: A Chinese word for a thing that arrived from abroad now has a set sound shape of its own and is used without anybody thinking of where it came from. Which description fits that word?

options.text: It is a loanword that has been fitted to the sound patterns and syllables of the borrowing language and has become ordinary
It is a translation that puts a native word in place of the foreign one, so its sounds are native by construction
options.misconception: describes a translation, in which nothing foreign is ever said and so no sound has to be fitted

options.text: It is a dialect form that spread across the country once the dialects were standardised in the twentieth century
options.misconception: describes the standardisation of varieties rather than the settling of borrowed material

options.text: It is a compound built from two native words, which is how a language builds a word for something it has never seen before
options.misconception: describes coining by compounding, which is the usual route only when no loan exists at all

questions.explanation: A loanword travels through a sound system that will not accept it unchanged, so it arrives modified, and the modifications are predictable enough to be worth describing. Syllables that do not exist in the borrowing language are replaced with ones that do, consonant clusters that are impossible are broken up, and the tones of the original are replaced by tones in the receiving system. What comes out the far end sounds foreign if a speaker stops to think about it, and what is actually the test of a settled loanword is that nobody does. The keyed answer names both halves of that, the fitting and the becoming ordinary, and the second half is the important one, because a word that is still recognisably foreign is one whose users know the loan happened. The distractors describe three real processes and none of them applies here. B is a translation, and a translated word has no foreign sounds at all because nothing foreign was said. C is the standardisation of varieties rather than of borrowed material. D is a genuine way to coin a name, and a compound built from native words is the usual answer when no loan exists.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the sounds of the original, and then ask what tells a reader the word has stopped being foreign.
