questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: trace a four-character idiom to the episode it came from
questions.stem: A learner meets a four-character idiom and asks what the four characters mean separately. Which statement about that question is correct?

options.text: The four characters usually do not mean four separate things, because the phrase came from a single episode and the meaning grew out of the whole
The four characters do mean four separate things, and a learner who cannot parse them has not yet understood the phrase
options.misconception: expects a parse that was thrown away when the phrase was compressed, so the learner is judged as behind when the phrase has no inside

options.text: The four characters are all still used in modern speech, and the phrase is a polite way of using four ordinary words together
options.misconception: assumes the individual characters are what the phrase consists of, when they are usually ordinary words unrelated to it

options.text: The four characters mean one thing in a story and another in conversation, so the learner has to learn both before either makes sense
options.misconception: confuses a loose usage with a second meaning, and a phrase used loosely is still one phrase with one core sense

questions.explanation: Almost every chengyu began as a story and was compressed, and the compression is what makes them hard. A phrase drawn from an episode in a historical text keeps the four characters that were memorable in the original and loses the situation, so the characters function as an address rather than as a description. This is why competent adult native speakers also cannot usually account for the individual characters in an idiom they use fluently, and a learner who expects four glossable items is looking for something that was thrown away when the phrase was shortened. The keyed answer is right about both halves, that the characters are not separate meanings and that the phrase is the residue of a single episode. The distractors each promise a parse that does not exist. B is the expectation that produces the false belief that a learner is behind when in fact the phrase has no inside. C is wrong in a way worth noticing, because the individual characters are very often ordinary words with meanings that have nothing to do with the phrase. D is the account of a usage difference learners confuse with a meaning difference, and a phrase used loosely is still one fixed phrase with one core sense.
questions.hint: Ask what the phrase was before it became four characters, and whether a fluent speaker can gloss the characters one by one.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: What happens in a traditional festival
questions.learningObjective: state the practice that belongs to a named festival
questions.stem: A learner is asked what people actually do during a festival, rather than when it falls. Which pairing of festival and practice is correct?

options.text: At the Lantern Festival people hang lanterns and eat sweet soup, and the round shapes stand for family reunion
At the Dragon Boat Festival people exchange gifts of tea, and the giving is what marks the end of the fifth month
options.misconception: attaches a practice from a different occasion, and the fifth lunar month is remembered for what else happens in it

options.text: At the Mid-Autumn Festival people eat dumplings, which is the northern habit the festival is named for
options.misconception: moves a new-year dish onto the autumn festival, a confusion the two family occasions make easy

options.text: At the Spring Festival people sit outside watching the sky, because that is when the first star of the year appears
options.misconception: replaces a festival with an act of watching, when the new year is spent indoors around a table

questions.explanation: A festival is a set of practices, and the practices are what a learner should be able to name, since a date tells a reader nothing about what to expect. The Lantern Festival closes the first month of the year, and its practices are lanterns in the street and a sweet soup, the roundness of both standing for the reunion the season is marking. The other three each attach a real practice to the wrong festival, and they are attached in a way that is worth understanding rather than merely correcting. B is the practice of a different occasion, and the fifth lunar month is remembered for the other thing that happens in it. C mistakes the northern habit of eating dumplings at the new year for the autumn festival, and the mistake is understandable, because both are the food people most associate with a family occasion. D has replaced a festival with an act of watching, and the Spring Festival is the one festival whose practices happen indoors around a table, which is the opposite of the picture.
questions.hint: Ask what people do, and then ask what shape or feature of the practice the festival is marking.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: A regional dish and its ingredients
questions.learningObjective: match a regional dish to the ingredients that identify its region
questions.stem: A reader sees a dish described in one line and wants to know which region it belongs to. Which pairing of dish and identifying ingredient is right?

options.text: A boiled dumpling dish from the north, where the wrapper is thin and wheat flour does the work that rice does in the south
A rice dish from the south, where a wheat wrapper is used because wheat does not grow in the wetter south
options.misconception: asserts an agricultural fact, and cooking follows what grows far less neatly than this implies

options.text: A wheat-noodle dish from the north, identified by the same rice that identifies every northern dish
options.misconception: gives the right region with the wrong identifying item, which is a failure of the mechanism rather than of the fact

options.text: A rice-noodle dish from the south, identified by the wheat flour that has been the northern staple since the earliest period
options.misconception: gives the wrong item again and adds a historical claim about flour that the cooking does not support

questions.explanation: Regional cooking in China is organised largely around one substitution, and once a learner has it the dish names start to sort themselves. Wheat in the north, rice in the south, and almost every regional difference in a dish name is downstream of that. Dumplings, steamed buns and hand-rolled noodles are the northern family because they are built on a wheat wrapper or dough, and the southern family is built on rice, whether it is steamed, in a soup or stir-fried as a noodle. The keyed answer states the dumpling case and names the cause, which is climate and therefore what will grow rather than what will not. The distractors each break the link in a different way. B asserts that wheat does not grow in the south, which is a claim about agriculture rather than about cooking, and cooking does not follow agriculture that neatly. C gives the right region and then the wrong identifying item, which is a failure of the mechanism rather than of the fact. D does the same and adds a claim about the earliest period, which is a historical assertion with nothing in the cooking to support it.
questions.hint: Ask which staple the dish is built on, and then ask what the climate decides about which staple that is.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: A literary period and its concern
questions.learningObjective: state the concern characterising a literary period as a historical fact
questions.stem: A learner is asked which concern characterises a named literary period, and the question is about history rather than about taste. Which pairing is right?

options.text: The period is associated with writing that examined the scholar-official and the world of official life, and the concern is stated as a historical observation
The period is associated with writing that avoided politics entirely, because the writers of the period were not permitted to mention it
options.misconception: converts sustained interest in official life into a prohibition, and a prohibition would have produced silence

options.text: The period is associated with long narrative poems about travel, because the long poem was the period's only recognised form
options.misconception: takes one form and makes it the only form, confusing what a period is remembered for with what it could do

options.text: The period is associated with drama written for the stage, because theatre was the only medium the period's writers used
options.misconception: repeats the same confusion with a second form, and turns a historical claim into a decorative one

questions.explanation: A period's characteristic concern is a statement about what writers in that period took as their material, and it is a historical claim that can be supported with dates and texts. The keyed pairing is the standard one: a concern with the scholar-official and with official life, examined from inside rather than from outside, which is what a reader means when the period is said to look at the world of the scholar and the bureaucracy. Stated as an observation rather than a verdict, it is also falsifiable, since a reader can go and check the poems. The distractors each assert something about the period that is not the case, and each has a shape worth recognising. B converts a period's interest in official life into a prohibition, and a prohibition would produce silence rather than the sustained attention that actually exists. C takes one form and makes it the only form, and long narrative poetry belongs to a different period. D does the same with drama, and the error in both is the same: confusing what a period is remembered for with what it was capable of, which is the confusion that turns a historical claim into a decorative one.
questions.hint: Ask what writers in the period took as their material, and ask whether the claim could be checked against a text.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: An author and a work as historical fact
questions.learningObjective: report an author and a work without turning the report into a judgement
questions.stem: A learner has to write one sentence giving a named author, one of that author's works, and one fact about the author that the work does not show. Explain what makes such a sentence historical rather than evaluative, and say what the learner must leave out.

answer.exemplar: The sentence is historical when each of its three parts could be checked against a record and none of them asks for approval. The author and the work are attributions, and their only requirement is accuracy, which means the title has to be the one the author actually wrote and the dates have to be the ones on the record. The third part is the one learners get wrong, and what is wanted there is a fact about the author's life or circumstances, such as where they were born, what their family situation was, or what a post held them in, and each of those is a matter of record. What has to be left out is any word of appraisal that is not a fact: the longest, the finest, the most moving, the most representative. Those words make the sentence an opinion wearing the shape of a sentence, and they fail a different test from a fact, because a reader who disagrees cannot check them and can only answer with a competing opinion. The two kinds of error are also different in what they do to a reader. A wrong fact misleads and can be corrected. An appraisal misleads about nothing, and it misleads about the writer, because a student who has learned to attach a superlative to every author has learned a habit that will carry into sentences about people and about events. A workable test for the learner is to read the finished sentence and ask of each clause whether a reader could contradict it with a record. Where the answer is yes, keep the clause. Where the answer is no, it is either an appraisal or a summary, and both have to go.

questions.explanation: The exemplar is marked as correct for separating the three kinds of clause, for naming the superlatives that have to go, and for giving a test the learner can apply unaided. A response that only says to avoid opinions has not told the learner what an opinion looks like inside a historical sentence, which is the part the question asks for.
questions.hint: Ask of each clause whether a reader could contradict it with a record, and rewrite one that could not be.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: state where a musical genre came from as a historical fact
questions.stem: A learner is asked where a musical genre developed, and the answer has to be a place and a period rather than a feeling. Which pairing is factually right?

options.text: A genre associated with the cities of the south-west in the early twentieth century, in music halls and dance halls for urban workers
A genre associated with the imperial court from the eighth century, performed by court musicians for the emperor
options.misconception: gives a real court origin to a genre made for urban workers, and the two audiences impose opposite constraints

options.text: A genre associated with the northern plains from the Qing dynasty, carried by travelling singers between villages
options.misconception: gives the folk pattern of transmission by people on foot, which favours long stanzas and small repertoires

options.text: A genre associated with overseas Chinese communities in the twentieth century, brought back from a foreign port
options.misconception: describes music that travelled back from abroad, and a learner should always ask whether a music was made here or brought here

questions.explanation: Popular genres are urban inventions, and knowing why a genre emerged in cities rather than in courts or villages answers most questions about its sound. A music that was made for workers in a city, played in halls they could reach after work, has to be danceable, repeatable and easy to hear over noise, and those constraints explain most of what a listener notices in it. The keyed answer gives the region, the period, and the setting, and the setting is the part that does the explanatory work. The distractors each offer a real and well-known origin and attach it to the wrong genre. The court music in the second option belongs to an earlier period and was made for a small audience in a palace, which is a completely different set of constraints from a public hall. The third is the folk pattern, carried by people on foot between settlements, and folk transmission favours long stanzas and small repertoires. The fourth describes music that did travel back from abroad, and a genre that arrived from a port has features of a different origin, which is why a learner should learn to ask whether a music was made here or brought here.
questions.hint: Ask who the music was made for, and where that audience could hear it, and what those two facts force the music to sound like.

questions.learningObjective: order the turns of a disagreement that does not damage the group
questions.stem: Four lines from a disagreement in a group chat have to be put back into order. Only one sequence keeps the disagreement between the ideas and not between the people. Which sequence is it?

options.text: 我有个不同的看法，不过前两位说的我听明白了。 / 我担心这样改会影响下个月的进度。 / 要不我们先试两周，再一起看看结果。 / 谢谢你们听我说完，我会把担心写成一段发过来。

The first move is to establish that the disagreement is an addition rather than an attack, and the keyed line does two jobs at once: it names a different view and it concedes that the other two were heard, which is the part that stops the next line from sounding like a rebuttal. Only then does the substance arrive, stated as a worry about a consequence rather than as a verdict on the plan, and a worry is much easier to agree or disagree with than a verdict. The proposal comes third, because a group cannot move to a next step until there is one, and the offer of a small trial is what makes the disagreement cheap. The thank-you comes last, since thanking people for listening is a closing move and putting it early would be a way of ending the conversation. The other orders each break a dependency. The second opens with the worry before anyone has agreed to discuss it, which makes the worry an interruption. The third proposes a resolution before the reason for it exists, so the group cannot accept it. The fourth thanks people for a conversation that has not happened.
questions.hint: Ask which line has to precede the others before the group will treat what follows as an addition rather than as a rebuttal.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: A claim a platform's own design contradicts
questions.learningObjective: find the design fact that defeats a claim about a platform's effect
questions.stem: Stage one: a company says its feed helps people find topics they care about, and its own instructions tell users to follow topics and turn on notifications. Diagnose why the claim does not follow from that design. Stage two: state what evidence would be needed before the claim could be made, and say what the design makes unlikely.

answer.exemplar: Stage one. The design contradicts the claim because the design measures persistence rather than satisfaction. Following a topic is one of the few unambiguous signals available, because it is a deliberate act a user performs and a system can count exactly, and a notification is a channel designed to bring the user back rather than to tell the user when something has finished. A feed tuned to a signal like that will keep finding more to show, and finding more is what the optimisation is for. A topic a person has followed once is now a standing instruction to show more, and the system has no way of reading the fact that the second, third and fourth items in that topic were not what the person wanted. The company has therefore described an outcome it does not measure: it has a system for measuring whether somebody came back, and the word the claim needs is enjoyment, which appears nowhere in the design. The deeper diagnosis is the one already established about recommendation systems, and it applies here in the company's own favour, since the drift away from a stated purpose is not a bug in the design but the result of optimising the one thing the design can count. Stage two. The evidence needed is a measure of the second kind, and it has to come from the people using it rather than from the platform. A survey asking whether the feed surfaces what they want, taken at intervals rather than once, is the obvious instrument, and a better one asks about specific sessions rather than about the feed in general, because a general answer is an answer about habit. A holding measure of how long somebody stays on a deliberately chosen item would be stronger still. What the design makes unlikely is the dull finding, which is that once a person has followed a topic the platform has a standing reason to keep feeding it whether or not the feed is doing them any good, so the two things the survey would need to separate, persistence and satisfaction, are being driven apart by the design itself.

questions.explanation: The pairing tests a diagnosis and a remedy. The exemplar is marked as correct for naming the signal the design actually measures, for explaining why following a topic creates a standing instruction to show more, and for pointing out that the survey evidence has to come from users rather than from the platform. A response that only says the claim is unproven has diagnosed the gap without locating the mechanism that causes it.
questions.hint: Ask what the design can count, then ask what word the claim needs that the design never measures, and who would have to supply it.

questions.learningObjective: use an idiom in an original sentence the way speakers use one
questions.stem: A learner wants to use 画蛇添足 to say that somebody made a situation worse. Which sentence uses the idiom the way a speaker does?

options.text: 大家都已经走了，他还留下来把桌子擦了一遍，真是画蛇添足。
大家都已经走了，他画蛇添足地把桌子擦了一遍，很好。
options.misconception: attaches the idiom to a verb with a particle and then praises the act, which cancels the meaning the idiom carries

options.text: 大家都已经走了，他还留下来，真是画蛇添足过了。
options.misconception: puts the particle for past experience after the idiom, which no idiom takes, since the phrase is a comment and not a verb

options.text: 大家都已经走了，他还留下来把桌子擦了一遍，画蛇添足。
options.misconception: uses the idiom as a bare label with no evaluative clause, so a reader has to supply the judgement the phrase normally delivers

It normally closes a clause, and it carries an evaluation inside itself, which is why the keyed sentence needs nothing after it. A learner who has learned the literal story often treats it as a verb and hangs it on the action, which is what B does, and B also demonstrates a second habit worth naming: the contradiction. The phrase means the opposite of the judgement that follows it, and a reader who has been told something is unnecessary and then told it was good has to decide which of the two to believe. C reaches for the particle for past experience because the sentence is about something that happened, and it cannot go there, since the idiom is not the part of the sentence carrying the tense. D is the failure that produces the flat register: the phrase can be used as a label in ordinary speech, and a learner who does it in writing produces a sentence that is technically right and carries none of the force.
questions.hint: Ask whether the idiom is acting as a verb or as a comment, and whether anything after it agrees with what it means.

questions.learningObjective: distinguish a list a reader asked for from a list the reader did not
questions.stem: A reader types a query and gets a page of results, and on another site gets a page with no query at all. Which statement about the two pages is sound?

options.text: The first is ranked on the words the reader supplied and the reader can see why, and the second is ranked on behaviour the reader has already produced
The two are ranked by the same process, so an item appearing in one of them will also appear in the other
options.misconception: claims one result set predicts the other, which would only hold if the two processes were the same

options.text: The first is the one that can carry advertising and the second cannot, since a feed has no room for a paid result
options.misconception: asserts an advertising difference that belongs to neither model and separates nothing

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: tell the two genres apart by what each is measuring
questions.stem: A reader treats a review of a restaurant and a fact-check of a claim about that restaurant as the same kind of judgement. Explain the difference between the two in terms of what each is measuring, and say why a reader should not use one to settle the other.

answer.exemplar: The two are measuring different things and, more importantly, they are answering questions the other one cannot answer. A review reports one person's experience of an encounter and is a description of that encounter: what the reviewer ordered, what arrived, what it cost, what happened when they asked for something. Its reliability is bounded by everything that bounds a single encounter, including who the reviewer is and what they wanted from the evening. A fact-check measures the fit between a specific statement and specific material, and it reports that fit, including the cases where the material does not support the statement. It says nothing about the restaurant except what the checked statement was about. That is why neither settles the other, and the confusion runs in both directions. A reader who takes a fact-check as a review will conclude that a restaurant is good or bad from a paragraph about a claim, and the paragraph may not even have been about the food. A reader who takes a review as a fact-check will conclude that a claim about the restaurant must be true because enough people enjoyed a meal there, which is a mistake about what a crowd of diners establishes. The useful habit to teach is a question about kind before a question about content: ask first what the piece is measuring, and only then what it found. Two reviews that disagree are usually two experiences, and two fact-checks that disagree are usually two claims. Neither disagreement tells a reader which of them is right, and the piece that would settle it is usually a third piece of a different kind entirely.

A response that only says a review is opinion misses the structural difference, which is the boundedness of what an encounter can establish.
questions.hint: Ask what each piece is measuring, and then ask what a third kind of piece would be needed to settle a disagreement between them.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: use the verb in a headline to judge what the report is claiming
questions.stem: A learner reads only headlines and has noticed that two reports of the same event use different verbs. Explain what a headline's verb tells the reader, and give the learner a way to use it rather than merely to notice it.

answer.exemplar: The verb is the part of a headline that does the most work, and it is the part a reader trained to skim skips, because a skim reads nouns and a noun can be true of the story whichever verb was chosen. What a verb carries is the relationship between the actors and the event. A verb that puts an actor first as the subject of a plain action reports the action without assigning it, and a verb that puts an actor first with a negation assigns it to somebody. A verb of planning or intending reports something that has not happened, and a reader who treats it as a report of an event has read a report of an intention as a report of a fact. A verb of causation claims that one thing produced another, which is a much stronger claim than sequence and is the one most often unsupported. The way to use this rather than merely notice it is to make the reader ask one question of every headline and to apply it in the same order: who or what is the subject, what exactly does the verb assert has happened or not happened, and does the sentence say anybody caused it. A learner who answers those three in order will find that a single headline sometimes fails on the third, and that the failure is a fact about the evidence rather than about the reader's understanding. The training to pair with it is to open two or three reports of one event and compare their verbs before reading any of the bodies. The comparison is quick and it is decisive, because when two reports describe the same occurrence and choose different verbs, the difference is in what each report is willing to assert, and that is usually where the reporting and the interest are. What this is not is a licence to distrust every headline. Most verbs are chosen accurately, and the exercise is about the cases where the choice is doing more than reporting, which is a smaller number and a more interesting one.

The mechanism explains the pattern without needing an intention, so the claim of intention is an addition. A learner who has understood the mechanism will be in danger here, because the mechanism makes the claim feel confirmed: the prediction came true, so the story must be right. That is the trap, and it is worth naming as a general hazard rather than as a mistake in this sentence, because it is the way a correct mechanism gets used to support a claim the mechanism does not reach. The first is the friend's own account of what they have been shown, since the learner is working from a fraction of a feed neither of them can hold in mind, and the friend may turn out to be choosing the other material as deliberately. That version is checkable, it does not accuse a platform that cannot be asked, and it puts the next step where it belongs, with the person who can answer it. It is direct, vivid, and often the only record that anything went wrong at all, and a reader who dismisses it on the grounds that it cannot be verified will dismiss the experiences that are hardest to document. It is also a person's account of their own experience, which means memory, motive and audience all bear on it, and none of those make it false. The keyed answer draws the line in the right place: the account is worth reading as a report of what happened to the person who wrote it, and it does not by itself establish anything about the institution the person is describing, because one experience and an institution are different objects. The distractors each push to an extreme. B is the argument from sincerity, and sincerity is a claim about motives rather than about accuracy, and a person who believes what they are saying is not thereby right about a pattern. C is the position that will lead a reader to ignore the most important material about a place. D is the mirror image, and it is wrong for a reason worth knowing: a first-person account is exactly as editable after the fact as a document is, and the belief that speech is harder to forge is part of what makes a manufactured recording work.
questions.hint: Ask what the account is evidence about, and then ask which object it is being made to stand in for.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: What a follower count does not measure
questions.learningObjective: identify the limits of a number that looks like a measure of standing
questions.stem: An account is described in a paragraph as having two hundred thousand followers, and the paragraph treats the number as a measure of reliability. Which correction is right?

options.text: The number measures how many accounts chose to subscribe, which says something about reach and nothing about whether the content can be trusted
The number measures how many people read the posts, since a subscription requires having read at least one of them
options.misconception: confuses a subscription with an act of reading, which is not required and is not implied by it

options.text: The number is a reliable proxy for accuracy, because an account with a large following is one that many people have checked at length
options.misconception: asserts the claim under examination, and nothing in a count says the account was ever checked

options.text: The number is unreliable in a way that a reader can correct by counting the comments, since comments are harder to obtain than subscriptions
options.misconception: swaps one weak signal for another, since comments can be coordinated as easily as subscriptions

questions.explanation: A follower count is a count of a particular action and nothing else, and the error is treating the number as a measurement of a different thing. Subscribing is cheap, it is often done without reading, and an account can accumulate a very large number of them without any of the people ever checking anything. What the number does measure is reach, which is a real and useful quantity: it tells a reader how many accounts are in a position to see the next post. The keyed answer holds the two apart, reach on one side and trust on the other, and the reason that separation matters is that reach can be used well. B confuses a subscription with an act of reading, which is not required and is not implied. C is the claim under examination, and it is unsupported, because nothing about a count tells a reader whether the account has been checked or has simply accumulated. D proposes a correction, and the correction is wrong in a way worth stating: comments can be bought or coordinated at least as easily as subscriptions, so they are not a firmer measure, and a reader who tries to substitute one weak signal for another has gained nothing.
questions.hint: Ask what action the number counts, and then ask whether a reader who performed that action checked anything.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: A notification and the decision it forces
questions.learningObjective: identify the decision a notification pushes a reader towards
questions.stem: An account is set to send a notification whenever it posts, and the reader finds that they open it each time without deciding to. Which statement describes the situation accurately?

options.text: A notification moves the decision to a moment the reader did not choose, and acting on it is a reaction rather than a choice
A notification saves time by bringing the post to the reader, so the reader has in effect requested it by subscribing
options.misconception: inverts the relationship, since a subscription was a decision about following and not about being interrupted

options.text: A notification is delivered only to readers who have already opened the post once, so it arrives after a decision rather than replacing one
options.misconception: states a delivery rule that is backwards, since a prompt is most effective before any opening

options.text: A notification has no effect on what a reader opens, since a reader can always ignore one and always does
options.misconception: assumes rather than tests the claim, and the observation is that a person who was not choosing reports acting anyway

questions.explanation: A notification works by changing when a decision is available, and that is enough to change the decision itself. The difference between a reader choosing to open a feed and a reader receiving a prompt and opening the account is the difference between acting on a purpose and reacting to a stimulus, and the mechanism is not persuasion so much as timing: a prompt arrives at a moment when the cost of responding is one tap. The keyed answer describes that accurately and without overstating it, because the reader still has the tap available to decline. The distractors each rescue the notification by giving it a purpose it does not have. B calls it a convenience and treats a subscription as a request for a prompt, which inverts the relationship, since the subscription was a decision about following and not about being interrupted. C states a delivery rule that is backwards, since a prompt is at its most effective before any opening. D is the optimistic reading, and it is the one a reader who wants to believe the arrangement is benign will prefer, and it is also the reading that has to be tested rather than assumed, because the point of the observation is that a person who was not choosing reports acting anyway.
questions.hint: Ask who chose the moment, and then ask what a one-tap response to that moment amounts to.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: state what a trending label records and what produced it
questions.stem: A term appears beside every video for three hours and then stops. Which statement about the label is sound?

options.text: The label records volume of activity in a recent window, so it reports that something happened quickly rather than that it is important
The label marks the term as the subject of most concern among editors, so it identifies what ought to be read
options.misconception: converts a volume measurement into an editorial judgement, and no editor is involved in a count

options.text: The label is applied once a term has been checked against a list of false claims, so its presence is a form of certification
options.misconception: reads the label as a check, which is the belief that lets a trending false claim pass as vetted

options.text: The label means the term is new, since a term already in wide use cannot be trending again
options.misconception: assumes a term cannot return, when in a cycle of events the same phrase comes back repeatedly

questions.explanation: A trending label is a measurement and the measurement is a rate, which is why the three hours matter as much as the count. What the label says is that activity on this term has been unusually high in a short recent window, and a rate is exactly the quantity that a burst of sharing can produce without anything having changed underneath. That is the whole reason the label is worth understanding rather than just reading, because the intuition it produces, that something has become important, is not what was measured. The distractors each attach a purpose the label does not have. B converts a volume measurement into an editorial judgement, and no editorial judgement is involved in a figure produced by counting. C is the most damaging reading, because a user who believes the label is a check will treat a trending false claim as vetted, and the label certifies nothing at all. D is wrong in a way that is easy to correct and easy to forget: a term can be returned to, and in a cycle of events it very often is, which is why the same phrase appears in these lists more than once a year.
questions.hint: Ask what quantity the label is measuring, over what window, and what a burst of sharing would do to it.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: A recording as evidence for a live claim
questions.learningObjective: weigh a recording that was made after the event it describes
questions.stem: A person claims that a livestream in which they appeared contained something it did not contain, and produces a video to show it. Which statement about the video is sound?

options.text: A recording can be cut, reordered and re-voiced, so it is evidence of an edited version rather than of what the livestream contained
The video settles the matter, because a livestream is produced once and a later recording cannot depart from it
options.misconception: assumes a live signal is fixed forever, which is the belief that makes an edited recording convincing

options.text: The video cannot help at all, because anything a person produces about their own appearance is automatically untrustworthy
options.misconception: discards the best evidence about the event, since the person who was present is often the only witness

options.text: The video is stronger than a log, because a viewer can hear the speaker's own voice saying the disputed words
options.misconception: treats a familiar voice as a guarantee, when a voice can be extracted and reused and should prompt a second look

questions.explanation: The problem is that the evidence and the event come from different production processes. A livestream is a live signal, and what a viewer saw was one particular rendering of it at one moment. A recording made afterwards has been through several hands and several steps, and each of the obvious ones, cutting, reordering and replacing the audio, leaves a result that is still watchable and still fluent. So the recording is genuine evidence of a version, and the version is the one the person made. The keyed answer says exactly this and stops there, which is the right level of claim: it does not say the video is fabricated, only that it establishes less than the person wants it to. The distractors each overreach. B assumes a live signal is fixed forever, which is the belief that makes an edited recording convincing to the person who made it. C is the position that discards the best evidence about the event, since the person who was present is the only witness in many cases. D is the subtlest, because hearing somebody's own voice does feel like strong evidence and it is not: a voice can be extracted and reused, and a fluent recording of a person saying their own words is precisely the thing that should prompt a second look rather than a conclusion.
questions.hint: Ask what has to have happened to a recording between the event and the showing, and ask whether the person showing it could have done it.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.topic: A report and a claim about a report
questions.learningObjective: keep straight what a piece establishes and what a piece says about another piece
questions.stem: An article reports that a fact-check site has rated a claim false, and a reader concludes the claim is false. Which description of the two steps is accurate?

options.text: The article establishes what the site concluded, and what the claim is depends on whether the site's material was right
The article and the site together establish the claim is false, because a report of a ruling inherits the ruling's authority
options.misconception: makes a verdict self-propagating, which is how a repetition ends up being a reader's only evidence

options.text: Neither establishes anything, because a site that rates claims cannot have standing to do so
options.misconception: denies a site the standing to rate claims, and so licenses accepting any claim because somebody checked it

options.text: Only the site establishes the claim, because an article reporting a ruling is a repetition and adds no evidence
options.misconception: strips the article of all value, when a report of a check is itself checkable evidence

questions.explanation: Reporting on a check and performing the check are two different acts, and a reader who runs them together loses the ability to evaluate either. The article in the stem is evidence that a particular site reached a particular conclusion about a particular claim, and that is a real and checkable fact. Whether the claim is false is a further step, and it goes through the site's material rather than through the article, so a reader who wants to reach the second conclusion has to go and look at what the site compared. The keyed answer keeps the two apart and says what the second one depends on, which is the whole of the item. The distractors each collapse them. B is the inheritance argument, and it is the error that lets a verdict be repeated until it reaches a reader who has seen no evidence, at which point the repetition is all that is left. C denies a site the standing to rate claims, which is a decision about institutions rather than about evidence, and it would license a reader to accept any claim just because somebody checked it. D goes the other way and strips the article of all value, when a report of a check is itself evidence and is often the only report a reader will see.
questions.hint: Ask what the article is evidence about, and then ask what the second conclusion would require going to look at.
